title: Deep Quakes and Hot Spots: Moving Plates
subject: earth science
goal: Use real earthquake depths and island ages to find where one plate sinks under another, and how fast the Pacific Plate moves.
steps: Part 1, the Andes. Plot each earthquake depth from the first table on the board: distance east of the ocean trench across, depth down.
Connect your points. The Skeptic asks: what shape do the earthquakes make, and which way does it slope? (The depth axis is stretched about 2 times, so the real slope is gentler, about 30°.)
Together, sketch the sinking plate on the board. Label the ocean trench, the South American Plate, and the Nazca Plate going under it.
Pass the role cards left. Part 2, Hawaii. The Big Island sits over a hot spot. Use the second table: how far each island is from the hot spot, and how old its lava is.
Work out the plate's speed from Kauai: distance ÷ age. Turn km per million years into cm per year (1 km per million years = 0.1 cm per year). Record it in the table.

data.title: Earthquakes under the Andes, 20-24° S (USGS, magnitude 5 and up, 2000-2025: the middle depth in each band); shallow quakes inside the South American Plate, 650-750 km east, are left out
The Hawaiian Islands (USGS ages of each island's main lava)

listen_for: Plotting depth upward instead of downward. The Skeptic checks the board's axis.
“The hot spot moves.” Ask: if the hot spot stays put, what must be moving?
Units: km per million years versus cm per year.
debrief: Ask: why are there deep earthquakes on only one side of the trench?
Ask: 10 cm a year is about two to three times as fast as fingernails grow. How far has Honolulu moved since you were born?
sources: Earthquakes: USGS earthquake catalog (earthquake.usgs.gov), events of magnitude 5 and up between 20° and 24° S, 2000-2025, grouped in 50 km bands. Island ages: USGS. The idea is also explored in PhET's Plate Tectonics and the Concord Consortium's Seismic Explorer. The activity and questions were written for Paper Loop.
